newsitem.title: USA: PacifiCorp deal runs afoul of U.K.'s Labour.
newsitem.headline: PacifiCorp deal runs afoul of U.K.'s Labour.

text.p: British officials Friday announced an investigation of PacifiCorp's friendly bid for Energy Group Plc , the latest sign from Britain's new Labour government that it will take a less laissez-faire policy toward utilities.

The move, which marks the first time a U.S. takeover of a British electricity company has been sent to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC) for further consideration, sent shares of Energy Group plunging 33.5 pence to 617.5p and pushed PacifiCorp stock down 62.5 cents to $21.6875.
Industry analysts said the delay does not mean the $9.6 billion stock and debt deal is off, but it shows the Labour Government is going to be less tolerant of foreign takeovers.
"They seem to be saying 'Watch out the U.K. might not be for sale anymore'," Daniele Seitz, a utility analyst at UBS Securities, said.
After being privatized in 1990 under the previous Tory government, all but one of Britain's 12 regional electricity companies have been swallowed by merger partners.
Seven of those deals involved U.S. buyers such as Central & Southwest Corp, American Electric Power and Public Service Co of Colorado
The U.S. utilities cited trans-Atlantic synergies in power supply, technology and generation for the mergers.
Increasing scrunity from the U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) of utility mergers within the U.S. has led some companies to look overseas.
After a surge in U.S. mergers about three years ago, lengthy FERC reviews, sometimes lasting two years or more, have stifled the trend, analysts said.

The U.K. will begin to open its retail electricity market to competition in April, while in the U.S., California will become the first state to end electric utility monopolies when its market is opened in January.

The Labour government, which swept to power in a landslide victory on May 1, has been fiercely critical of the previous goverment's takeover policy and in late June launched a major review of utilities regulation.
The government also vowed to levy a one-time tax on windfall profits of privatized utilities in its first budget.
In mid-June, PacifiCorp announced plans to acquire Energy Group, which was formed in February through the spin off Hanson Plc's energy assets.
Analysts hailed the deal as a combination of two highly competitive electricity generators that seemed to have common visions for exploiting opportunities in global energy markets.
Energy Group owns Eastern Electricity, the U.K.'s largest utility in terms of distribution territory, as well as Peabody Coal Co, the largest coal producer in the U.S.

Analysts said Friday the decision by Margaret Beckett, U.K. Trade and Industry Secretary, to refer the PacifiCorp/Energy Group deal to the country's Monopolies and Mergers Commission was fairly surprising.
"Obviously there is no possiblity of excess market power--there is an ocean between the two companies," Sietz at UBS noted.
She and others said the U.K. authorities were unlikely to be concerned about the combination of Peabody Coal with PacifiCorp's coal assets since those operations are mostly in the U.S. and Australia.
"Regulators will do what they want. Depending on what the outcome is, the value of the deal could change," said Linda Byus, an analyst at Nesbitt Burns Securities.
PacifiCorp spokesman Dave Kvamme said the company was disappointed by plans for an investigation, which is scheduled to finish in late November.
"Presuming a positive outcome of the Monopolies and Mergers Commission review and approval from Margaret Beckett...we expect to submit another bid (for Energy Group)," Kvamme said.
Earlier this week, PacifiCorp announced holders representing almost two-thirds of Energy Group share capital had accepted the 690-pence-per-share offer.
But that offer is now on hold, said Kvamme.
PacifiCorp Friday said it would cooperate fully in the inquiry and respond promptly to information requests by the U.K. commission.

Kvamme said the company expected to find out over the next few days who will be involved in the investigation and what kind of information will be requested. Eventually, a formal hearing schedule would be set.
PacifiCorp noted the U.S. Federal Trade Commission had also requested time to consider additional information provided by the companies for its antitrust review.
